topics.title: Review of the basic trigonometric ratios
Finding angles using the cosine rule

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the known and unknown sides relative to each marked angle, select sine, cosine or tangent, and multiply by the known side. Rotated diagrams require side recognition but no linked construction.

content.prompt: Calculate the value of each pronumeral, correct to two decimal places.

spec.description: Horizontal base, vertical right leg and rising hypotenuse; right angle at bottom right.
spec.mathematics: Hypotenuse 14 cm; angle at bottom left 32 degrees; opposite leg a cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\sin32^\circ&=\frac{a}{14}\\a&=14\sin32^\circ\\a&\approx7.42\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right angle at upper left; short vertical left leg and horizontal upper leg.
spec.mathematics: Hypotenuse 12 cm; lower-left angle 72 degrees; adjacent leg b cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\cos72^\circ&=\frac{b}{12}\\b&=12\cos72^\circ\\b&\approx3.71\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Horizontal upper leg and vertical right leg; right angle at upper right.
spec.mathematics: Upper leg 5 m; upper-left angle 51 degrees; opposite leg c m.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\tan51^\circ&=\frac{c}{5}\\c&=5\tan51^\circ\\c&\approx6.17\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Horizontal lower hypotenuse; right angle at upper-left vertex.
spec.mathematics: Leg adjacent to rightmost 16-degree angle is 8 cm; opposite leg d cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\tan16^\circ&=\frac{d}{8}\\d&=8\tan16^\circ\\d&\approx2.29\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Inverted right triangle with horizontal upper hypotenuse and right angle at lower vertex.
spec.mathematics: Hypotenuse 4.8 cm; upper-left angle 47 degrees; opposite right leg i cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\sin47^\circ&=\frac{i}{4.8}\\i&=4.8\sin47^\circ\\i&\approx3.51\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right angle at upper vertex; lower hypotenuse rises slightly to the right.
spec.mathematics: Left leg 16.2 cm is adjacent to lower-left 40-degree angle; opposite right leg j cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\tan40^\circ&=\frac{j}{16.2}\\j&=16.2\tan40^\circ\\j&\approx13.59\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Calculate the value of the pronumeral, correct to two decimal places.

spec.description: Horizontal base, vertical right leg, hypotenuse rising from left to right; right angle at bottom right.
spec.mathematics: The side opposite 10 degrees is 2.6 cm; the hypotenuse is a cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\sin 10^\circ &= \frac{2.6}{a}\\a\sin 10^\circ &= 2.6\\a &= \frac{2.6}{\sin 10^\circ}\\a &\approx 14.97\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Vertical left leg, horizontal top leg, hypotenuse rising from bottom left to top right; right angle at top left.
spec.mathematics: The side opposite 51 degrees is 7 cm; the hypotenuse is b cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\sin 51^\circ &= \frac{7}{b}\\b\sin 51^\circ &= 7\\b &= \frac{7}{\sin 51^\circ}\\b &\approx 9.01\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Vertical left leg and horizontal bottom leg; descending hypotenuse; right angle at bottom left.
spec.mathematics: The side adjacent to 40 degrees is 9 m; the hypotenuse is e m.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\cos 40^\circ &= \frac{9}{e}\\e\cos 40^\circ &= 9\\e &= \frac{9}{\cos 40^\circ}\\e &\approx 11.75\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Horizontal bottom hypotenuse and upper-right right-angle vertex; short right leg slopes down to the lower-right 71-degree vertex.
spec.mathematics: The side adjacent to 71 degrees is 12.6 cm; the hypotenuse is h cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\cos 71^\circ &= \frac{12.6}{h}\\h\cos 71^\circ &= 12.6\\h &= \frac{12.6}{\cos 71^\circ}\\h &\approx 38.70\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Complete right triangles by selecting side and inverse trigonometric ratios, using Pythagoras where appropriate and applying two rounding precisions.

content.prompt: Find all sides, correct to two decimal places, and all angles, correct to one decimal place.

spec.description: Vertical left leg, horizontal upper leg and rising diagonal; right angle at upper left and 40° at lower left. Unfilled black house-style reconstruction.
spec.mathematics: The vertical leg is 3 cm and is adjacent to the given 40° angle.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied 3 cm, 40° and right-angle marker are visible.

answer.short: Sides: $3\text{ cm}$, $2.52\text{ cm}$ and $3.92\text{ cm}$. Angles: $40.0^\circ$, $50.0^\circ$ and $90.0^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse, $x$ the horizontal side and $\alpha$ the remaining acute angle.
$$\begin{align*}
\cos40^\circ&=\frac{3}{h}\\
h\cos40^\circ&=3\\
h&=\frac{3}{\cos40^\circ}\\
h&\approx3.92\text{ cm}\\
\tan40^\circ&=\frac{x}{3}\\
x&=3\tan40^\circ\\
x&\approx2.52\text{ cm}\\
\alpha&=90^\circ-40^\circ\\
\alpha&=50.0^\circ
\end{align*}$$
The supplied side is $3\text{ cm}$; the other angles are $40.0^\circ$ and $90.0^\circ$.

spec.description: Right triangle with vertical left leg, horizontal base and diagonal descending from upper left to lower right; right angle at lower left. Unfilled black house-style reconstruction.
spec.mathematics: Vertical leg 6 cm; hypotenuse 9.2 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied lengths and the right-angle marker are visible.

answer.short: Sides: $6\text{ cm}$, $6.97\text{ cm}$ and $9.2\text{ cm}$. Angles: $40.7^\circ$, $49.3^\circ$ and $90.0^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the horizontal side, $\theta$ the lower-right angle and $\phi$ the upper-left angle.
$$\begin{align*}
x^2+6^2&=9.2^2\\
x^2&=9.2^2-6^2\\
x&=\sqrt{9.2^2-6^2}\\
x&\approx6.97\text{ cm}\\
\sin\theta&=\frac{6}{9.2}\\
\theta&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{6}{9.2}\right)\\
\theta&\approx40.7^\circ\\
\phi&=90^\circ-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{6}{9.2}\right)\\
\phi&\approx49.3^\circ
\end{align*}$$
The supplied sides are $6\text{ cm}$ and $9.2\text{ cm}$; the right angle is $90.0^\circ$.

spec.description: Triangle with horizontal lower hypotenuse and upper right-angle vertex; left sloping leg 5 cm and right sloping leg 8.4 cm. Unfilled black house-style reconstruction.
spec.mathematics: Perpendicular legs 5 cm and 8.4 cm; horizontal base is the hypotenuse.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied lengths and the upper right-angle marker are visible.

answer.short: Sides: $5\text{ cm}$, $8.4\text{ cm}$ and $9.78\text{ cm}$. Angles: $59.2^\circ$ at the lower left, $30.8^\circ$ at the lower right and $90.0^\circ$ at the top.
answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse, $\theta$ the lower-left angle and $\phi$ the lower-right angle.
$$\begin{align*}
h^2&=5^2+8.4^2\\
h&=\sqrt{5^2+8.4^2}\\
h&\approx9.78\text{ cm}\\
\tan\theta&=\frac{8.4}{5}\\
\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{8.4}{5}\right)\\
\theta&\approx59.2^\circ\\
\phi&=90^\circ-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{8.4}{5}\right)\\
\phi&\approx30.8^\circ
\end{align*}$$
The supplied sides are $5\text{ cm}$ and $8.4\text{ cm}$; the upper angle is $90.0^\circ$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Use SOHCAHTOA, substitute the supplied lengths or angle, rearrange for unknown sides, and use inverse trigonometric functions for unknown angles. Acute angles in a right triangle sum to 90°. Pythagoras supplies a missing side when two sides are known.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Page 2 defines the ratios and complementary angles; page 3 Example 2 demonstrates numerator and denominator side calculations; page 4 Example 3 demonstrates inverse trigonometry with one-decimal-place angles. Question 5 combines those methods to complete each triangle.

content.prompt: Find the exact value of $x$.

spec.description: Right triangle with vertical unknown side, horizontal base, descending hypotenuse and bottom-left right angle. Ordinary source blue strokes use house black.
spec.mathematics: Hypotenuse 10 cm; unknown x cm opposite 30 degrees.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\sin30^\circ&=\frac{x}{10}\\x&=10\sin30^\circ\\x&=10\times\frac12\\x&=5\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right triangle with horizontal unknown top side, vertical left side and diagonal hypotenuse; top-left right-angle marker.
spec.mathematics: Hypotenuse 12 cm; x cm adjacent to 45 degrees.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\cos45^\circ&=\frac{x}{12}\\x&=12\cos45^\circ\\x&=\frac{12}{\sqrt2}\\x&=\frac{12\sqrt2}{2}\\x&=6\sqrt2\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right triangle with horizontal base, vertical unknown right side and rising hypotenuse; bottom-right right angle.
spec.mathematics: Hypotenuse 12 mm; x mm opposite 60 degrees.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\sin60^\circ&=\frac{x}{12}\\x&=12\sin60^\circ\\x&=12\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\x&=6\sqrt3\text{ mm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right triangle with horizontal unknown top side and vertical right side; top-right right angle.
spec.mathematics: Side opposite 30 degrees is 4 cm; adjacent side is x cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\tan30^\circ&=\frac4x\\\frac4x&=\frac1{\sqrt3}\\x&=4\sqrt3\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Equilateral triangle with all three outer side labels retained, internal perpendicular altitude and right-angle marker at its foot. No midpoint ticks or angle labels added. Source altitude unit cm corrected to m to match metre givens and teacher result.
spec.mathematics: Three sides 8 m; altitude x m.
spec.answerVisibility: No calculated half-base, angle or height is supplied.

answer.worked:
The triangle is equilateral, so each angle is $60^\circ$. The altitude forms a right triangle with hypotenuse $8\text{ m}$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin60^\circ&=\frac{x}{8}\\x&=8\sin60^\circ\\x&=8\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\x&=4\sqrt3\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute exact trigonometric ratios into compound expressions, simplify surds and rationalise denominators.

content.prompt: Find the exact values, rationalising the denominator where appropriate.

children.label: a
children.prompt: $(\sin 60^\circ)^2+(\cos 60^\circ)^2$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}(\sin 60^\circ)^2+(\cos 60^\circ)^2&=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2+\left(\frac12\right)^2\\(\sin 60^\circ)^2+(\cos 60^\circ)^2&=\frac34+\frac14\\(\sin 60^\circ)^2+(\cos 60^\circ)^2&=1\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: $(\tan 30^\circ)^2-\dfrac{1}{(\cos 30^\circ)^2}$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}(\tan 30^\circ)^2-\frac{1}{(\cos 30^\circ)^2}&=\left(\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^2-\frac1{\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2}\\(\tan 30^\circ)^2-\frac{1}{(\cos 30^\circ)^2}&=\frac13-\frac1{3/4}\\(\tan 30^\circ)^2-\frac{1}{(\cos 30^\circ)^2}&=\frac13-\frac43\\(\tan 30^\circ)^2-\frac{1}{(\cos 30^\circ)^2}&=-1\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: $\dfrac{\tan60^\circ-\tan45^\circ}{1+\tan60^\circ\times\tan45^\circ}$

answer.short:
$2-\sqrt3$

Substitute the exact ratios and rationalise using the conjugate.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{\tan60^\circ-\tan45^\circ}{1+\tan60^\circ\times\tan45^\circ}&=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{1+\sqrt3\times1}\\\frac{\tan60^\circ-\tan45^\circ}{1+\tan60^\circ\times\tan45^\circ}&=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3+1}\times\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3-1}\\\frac{\tan60^\circ-\tan45^\circ}{1+\tan60^\circ\times\tan45^\circ}&=\frac{3-2\sqrt3+1}{3-1}\\\frac{\tan60^\circ-\tan45^\circ}{1+\tan60^\circ\times\tan45^\circ}&=\frac{4-2\sqrt3}{2}\\\frac{\tan60^\circ-\tan45^\circ}{1+\tan60^\circ\times\tan45^\circ}&=2-\sqrt3\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: $\sin45^\circ\times\cos60^\circ+\cos45^\circ\times\sin60^\circ$

answer.worked:
Using the exact ratios,
$$\begin{align*}\sin45^\circ\times\cos60^\circ+\cos45^\circ\times\sin60^\circ&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\times\frac12+\frac1{\sqrt2}\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\\sin45^\circ\times\cos60^\circ+\cos45^\circ\times\sin60^\circ&=\frac{1+\sqrt3}{2\sqrt2}\\\sin45^\circ\times\cos60^\circ+\cos45^\circ\times\sin60^\circ&=\frac{1+\sqrt3}{2\sqrt2}\times\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}\\\sin45^\circ\times\cos60^\circ+\cos45^\circ\times\sin60^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt2+\sqrt6}{4}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: $2\sin30^\circ\times\cos30^\circ$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}2\sin30^\circ\times\cos30^\circ&=2\times\frac12\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\2\sin30^\circ\times\cos30^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}2(\cos45^\circ)^2-1&=2\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)^2-1\\2(\cos45^\circ)^2-1&=2\times\frac12-1\\2(\cos45^\circ)^2-1&=0\end{align*}$$

Part c requires a conjugate because substitution produces a binomial denominator; this extends the printed rationalisation method without invoking trigonometric identities.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine rhombus diagonal properties with exact trigonometric ratios to find both diagonals.

content.prompt: $ABCD$ is a rhombus with $\angle ABD=30^\circ$. Find the exact length of each diagonal if the side lengths are $10\text{ cm}$.

answer.worked:
Let the diagonals intersect at $O$. The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so triangle $ABO$ is right-angled at $O$ and $\angle ABO=30^\circ$.

answer.worked:
In the smaller right triangle, $\tan45^\circ=1$, so its horizontal base is $x\ \mathrm{m}$. The larger triangle therefore has horizontal base $(x+100)\ \mathrm{m}$.

$$\begin{align*}

x&=\frac{100(\sqrt3+1)}{(\sqrt3-1)(\sqrt3+1)}\\
x&=\frac{100(\sqrt3+1)}{2}\\
x&=50(\sqrt3+1)\ \mathrm{m}.
\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the height of the tree, correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
Let $O$ be the base and $T$ the top of the tree. In the vertical right triangle $POT$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan32^\circ&=\frac{OT}{50}\\OT&=50\tan32^\circ\\OT&\approx31.2\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$
Retain $50\tan32^\circ$ for subsequent calculations.

children.label: b
children.prompt: $Q$ is a point 100 metres due east of $P$. Find:

children.label: i
children.prompt: the distance of $Q$ from the base of the tree

answer.worked:
Let $O$ be the base of the tree. Since north and east are perpendicular, $\angle OPQ=90^\circ$. By Pythagoras’ theorem:
$$\begin{align*}QO^2&=50^2+100^2\\QO^2&=12500\\QO&=50\sqrt5\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: the angle of elevation of the top of the tree from $Q$, correct to one decimal place

answer.worked:
Let $\theta=\angle TQO$, where $O$ and $T$ are the base and top of the tree. In the vertical right triangle $QOT$, use the unrounded height:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{OT}{QO}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{50\tan32^\circ}{50\sqrt5}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\tan32^\circ}{\sqrt5}\right)\\\theta&\approx15.6^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: the bearing of the tree from $Q$, correct to one decimal place

answer.worked:
Let $O$ be the base of the tree and $\alpha=\angle PQO$. The tree is north of west from $Q$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\alpha&=\frac{50}{100}\\\alpha&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right).\end{align*}$$
The clockwise bearing from north is:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Bearing}&=270^\circ+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)\\\text{Bearing}&\approx296.6^\circ\mathrm{T}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Dillon and Eugene are both looking at a tower of height 35 metres. Dillon is standing due south of the tower and he measures the angle of elevation from the ground to the top of the tower to be $15^\circ$. Eugene is standing due east of the tower and he measures the angle of elevation from the ground to the top of the tower to be $20^\circ$. Find, correct to one decimal place:

children.label: a
children.prompt: the distance Dillon is from the foot of the tower

answer.worked:
Let $O$ be the foot of the tower, $T$ its top, and $D$ Dillon's position. In the vertical right triangle $DOT$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan15^\circ&=\frac{35}{OD}\\OD&=\frac{35}{\tan15^\circ}\\OD&\approx130.6\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: the distance Eugene is from the foot of the tower

answer.worked:
Let $E$ be Eugene's position. In the vertical right triangle $EOT$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan20^\circ&=\frac{35}{OE}\\OE&=\frac{35}{\tan20^\circ}\\OE&\approx96.2\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: the distance between Dillon and Eugene

answer.worked:
Since Dillon is due south and Eugene due east of $O$, $\angle DOE=90^\circ$. Using the unrounded distances:
$$\begin{align*}DE^2&=OD^2+OE^2\\DE^2&=\left(\frac{35}{\tan15^\circ}\right)^2+\left(\frac{35}{\tan20^\circ}\right)^2\\DE&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{35}{\tan15^\circ}\right)^2+\left(\frac{35}{\tan20^\circ}\right)^2}\\DE&\approx162.2\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: the bearing of Dillon from Eugene

answer.short:
$216.4^\circ\text{T}$

Measure clockwise from north at Eugene's position.
answer.worked:
Let $\theta=\angle OED$, the angle south of west at Eugene's position. Using the unrounded distances:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{OD}{OE}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{35/\tan15^\circ}{35/\tan20^\circ}\right)\\\theta&\approx53.6^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The bearing is measured clockwise from north at $E$:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Bearing}&=270^\circ-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{35/\tan15^\circ}{35/\tan20^\circ}\right)\\\text{Bearing}&\approx216.4^\circ\text{T}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: From a point $A$, a lighthouse is on a bearing of $026^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$ and the top of the lighthouse is at angle of elevation of $20.5^{\circ}$. From a point $B$, the lighthouse is on a bearing of $296^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$ and the top of the lighthouse is at angle of elevation of $10.2^{\circ}$. If $A$ and $B$ are 500 metres apart, find the height of the lighthouse, correct to the nearest metre.

answer.short:
$81\text{ m}$

Use the bearings to identify a right-angled ground triangle, then combine Pythagoras’ theorem with the two tangent ratios.
answer.worked:
Let $O$ be the foot of the lighthouse, $T$ its top and $OT=h$ metres. The reverse bearings of $A$ and $B$ from $O$ are $206^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$ and $116^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$, so $\angle AOB=90^{\circ}$.

In the vertical right-angled triangles:
$$\begin{align*}\tan20.5^{\circ}&=\frac{h}{OA}\\OA&=\frac{h}{\tan20.5^{\circ}}\\\tan10.2^{\circ}&=\frac{h}{OB}\\OB&=\frac{h}{\tan10.2^{\circ}}\end{align*}$$
Applying Pythagoras’ theorem to the horizontal triangle $AOB$:
$$\begin{align*}OA^2+OB^2&=500^2\\\left(\frac{h}{\tan20.5^{\circ}}\right)^2+\left(\frac{h}{\tan10.2^{\circ}}\right)^2&=250000\\h^2\left(\frac{1}{\tan^220.5^{\circ}}+\frac{1}{\tan^210.2^{\circ}}\right)&=250000\\h&=\frac{500}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{\tan^220.5^{\circ}}+\frac{1}{\tan^210.2^{\circ}}}}\\h&\approx81.0655\end{align*}$$
The lighthouse is $81\text{ m}$ high, correct to the nearest metre.

content.prompt: From the top of a cliff that runs north–south, the angle of depression of a yacht, 200 metres out to sea and due east of the observer, is $20^\circ$. When the observer next looks at the yacht, he notices that it has sailed 150 metres parallel to the cliff.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the height of the cliff, correct to the nearest metre.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the cliff height in metres. The angle of elevation from the yacht equals the angle of depression.
$$\begin{align*}\tan20^\circ&=\frac{h}{200}\\h&=200\tan20^\circ\\h&\approx73\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$
Keep $200\tan20^\circ$ unrounded for subsequent parts.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the distance the yacht is from the observer after it has sailed 150 metres parallel to the cliff, correct to the nearest metre.

answer.short:
$260\text{ m}$

Use Pythagoras’ theorem in the horizontal plane, then in the vertical triangle.
answer.worked:
The yacht's motion parallel to the cliff is perpendicular to its initial 200 m eastward displacement. Let $r$ be its new horizontal distance from the foot of the cliff and $d$ its distance from the observer, both in metres.
$$\begin{align*}r^2&=200^2+150^2\\r&=250.\end{align*}$$
Using the unrounded cliff height,
$$\begin{align*}d^2&=250^2+(200\tan20^\circ)^2\\d&=\sqrt{250^2+(200\tan20^\circ)^2}\\d&\approx260\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the angle of depression of the yacht from the top of the cliff when it is in its new position, correct to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the new angle of depression. It equals the angle of elevation in the vertical right triangle with horizontal side 250 m.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{200\tan20^\circ}{250}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{200\tan20^\circ}{250}\right)\\\theta&\approx16^\circ.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A mast is held in position by means of two taut ropes running from the ground to the top of the mast. One rope is of length 40 metres and makes an angle of $58^\circ$ with the ground. Its anchor point with the ground is due south of the mast. The other rope is 50 metres long and its anchor point is due east of the mast. Find the distance, correct to the nearest metre, between the two anchor points.

answer.short:
$42\text{ m}$

Find the mast height and the two ground distances, then apply Pythagoras’ theorem between the anchors.
answer.worked:
Let $O$ be the foot of the mast, $T$ its top, $S$ the southern anchor and $E$ the eastern anchor. The vertical mast is perpendicular to the ground.

In $\triangle SOT$:
$$\begin{align*}\sin58^\circ&=\frac{OT}{40}\\OT&=40\sin58^\circ\\OS&=40\cos58^\circ\end{align*}$$
In $\triangle EOT$, by Pythagoras’ theorem:
$$\begin{align*}OE^2&=50^2-OT^2\\OE^2&=2500-(40\sin58^\circ)^2\end{align*}$$
Since south and east are perpendicular, $\angle SOE=90^\circ$. Keeping intermediate values unrounded:
$$\begin{align*}SE^2&=OS^2+OE^2\\SE^2&=(40\cos58^\circ)^2+2500-(40\sin58^\circ)^2\\SE&=\sqrt{(40\cos58^\circ)^2+2500-(40\sin58^\circ)^2}\\SE&\approx42.409977\text{ m}\\SE&\approx42\text{ m}\quad\text{(nearest metre)}\end{align*}$$

Let $P$, $S$ and $L$ represent Paul, Sayo and the landmark, respectively, with $PS=800\text{ m}$. The landmark is west of the north–south line through the hikers.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{PL}{\sin60^{\circ}}&=\frac{800}{\sin78^{\circ}}\\PL&=\frac{800\sin60^{\circ}}{\sin78^{\circ}}\\PL&\approx708\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

An archaeologist wishes to determine the height of an ancient temple. From a point $A$ at ground level, she measures the angle of elevation of $V$, the top of the temple, to be $37^\circ$.

She then walks $100\text{ m}$ towards the temple to a point $B$. From here, the angle of elevation of $V$ from ground level is $64^\circ$. Find:

spec.description: A, B and O lie on horizontal ground in that order, with V vertically above O. AV and BV meet at V. The 64-degree angle lies between BV and BO, exterior to triangle AVB. A right-angle square marks BOV. Ordinary source blue geometry uses house black.
spec.mathematics: Angle VAB is 37 degrees; angle VBO is 64 degrees; angle BOV is 90 degrees. AB is 100 m, given only in the stem.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and vertex labels appear; no calculated angles, lengths or height are shown.

children.label: a
children.prompt: $\angle AVB$

answer.worked:
The exterior angle at $B$ equals the sum of the opposite interior angles of $\triangle AVB$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle AVB+37^\circ&=64^\circ\\\angle AVB&=64^\circ-37^\circ\\\angle AVB&=27^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: $VB$, correct to two decimal places

answer.worked:
Apply the sine rule in $\triangle AVB$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{VB}{\sin37^\circ}&=\frac{100}{\sin27^\circ}\\VB&=\frac{100\sin37^\circ}{\sin27^\circ}\\VB&\approx132.56\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: $OV$, the height of the temple, to the nearest metre

answer.short:
$119\text{ m}$

Use $OV=VB\sin64^\circ$, retaining the unrounded value of $VB$.
answer.worked:
In right-angled $\triangle BOV$, retain the exact expression for $VB$ from part b.
$$\begin{align*}\sin64^\circ&=\frac{OV}{VB}\\OV&=VB\sin64^\circ\\OV&=\frac{100\sin37^\circ}{\sin27^\circ}\sin64^\circ\\OV&\approx119\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A hillside is inclined at $26^\circ$ to the horizontal. From the bottom of the hill, Alex observes a vertical tree whose base is $40\text{ m}$ up the hill from the point where Alex is standing. If the angle of elevation of the top of the tree is $43^\circ$ from the point where Alex is standing, find the height of the tree, correct to the nearest metre.

answer.short:
$16\text{ m}$.

Find the angles in the triangle formed by Alex, the tree base and its top, then apply the sine rule.
answer.worked:
Let $A$ be Alex's position, $B$ the tree base and $T$ its top. The hillside distance is $AB=40\text{ m}$. Since the tree is vertical:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAT&=43^\circ-26^\circ\\\angle BAT&=17^\circ\\\angle ABT&=90^\circ+26^\circ\\\angle ABT&=116^\circ\\\angle ATB&=180^\circ-17^\circ-116^\circ\\\angle ATB&=47^\circ.\end{align*}$$
By the sine rule:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{BT}{\sin17^\circ}&=\frac{40}{\sin47^\circ}\\BT&=\frac{40\sin17^\circ}{\sin47^\circ}\\BT&\approx16\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$
The tree is approximately $16\text{ m}$ tall, correct to the nearest metre.

content.prompt: A point $M$ is one kilometre due east of a point $C$. A hill is on a bearing of $028^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$ from $C$ and is $1.2\text{ km}$ from $M$. Find:

children.label: a
children.prompt: the bearing of the hill from $M$, correct to the nearest degree

answer.short:
$341^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$.

Use the sine rule to find the triangle angles, then measure the bearing clockwise from north at $M$.
answer.worked:
Let $H$ denote the hill. Since $CM$ is due east,
$$\begin{align*}\angle MCH&=90^{\circ}-28^{\circ}\\\angle MCH&=62^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Apply the sine rule in $CMH$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\sin\angle CHM}{1}&=\frac{\sin62^{\circ}}{1.2}\\\angle CHM&=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\sin62^{\circ}}{1.2}\right)\\\angle CHM&\approx47.37398358^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
The supplementary angle is impossible because it would make the triangle's angle sum exceed $180^{\circ}$. Keeping the unrounded angle,
$$\begin{align*}\angle CMH&=180^{\circ}-62^{\circ}-\angle CHM\\\angle CMH&\approx70.62601642^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
From $M$, $C$ is due west and $H$ lies north of west. Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}\text{Bearing of }H\text{ from }M&=270^{\circ}+\angle CMH\\\text{Bearing of }H\text{ from }M&\approx340.62601642^{\circ}\\\text{Bearing of }H\text{ from }M&\approx341^{\circ}\mathrm{T}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: the distance, correct to the nearest metre, between $C$ and the hill

answer.worked:
Using the unrounded value of $\angle CMH$ from part a, apply the sine rule:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{CH}{\sin\angle CMH}&=\frac{1.2}{\sin62^{\circ}}\\CH&=\frac{1.2\sin\angle CMH}{\sin62^{\circ}}\\CH&\approx1.282123732\text{ km}\\CH&\approx1282\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A rhombus $PQRS$ has side lengths $8\text{ m}$, and contains an angle of $128^\circ$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the length of the longer diagonal, correct to two decimal places.

answer.worked:
The longer diagonal is opposite the larger included angle, $128^\circ$. Let its length be $d_L$ metres.
$$\begin{align*}d_L^2&=8^2+8^2-2\times8\times8\cos128^\circ\\d_L^2&=128-128\cos128^\circ\\d_L&=\sqrt{128-128\cos128^\circ}\\d_L&\approx14.38\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the length of the shorter diagonal, correct to two decimal places.

answer.worked:
Adjacent angles of a rhombus are supplementary, so the other included angle is $180^\circ-128^\circ=52^\circ$. Let the shorter diagonal be $d_S$ metres.
$$\begin{align*}d_S^2&=8^2+8^2-2\times8\times8\cos52^\circ\\d_S^2&=128-128\cos52^\circ\\d_S&=\sqrt{128-128\cos52^\circ}\\d_S&\approx7.01\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the area of the rhombus, correct to two decimal places.

answer.worked:
The area of a rhombus is half the product of its diagonals. Use the unrounded diagonal lengths.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area}&=\frac12d_Ld_S\\\text{Area}&=\frac12\sqrt{128-128\cos128^\circ}\sqrt{128-128\cos52^\circ}\\\text{Area}&\approx50.43\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Prove the cosine rule when the included angle, $A$, is obtuse.

spec.description: Obtuse triangle ABC with external perpendicular BX to the extension of AC. X, A and C are collinear in that order. Corrected conventional side labels follow the preceding cosine-rule statement and the teacher proof.
spec.mathematics: AB=c, BC=a, AC=b, BX=h and XA=x. BX is perpendicular to XC; angle BAX=180 degrees minus A.
spec.answerVisibility: Only construction labels and givens appear; the proof remains in the answer.

answer.short:
$a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$.

Use the external altitude, Pythagoras’ theorem and $\cos(180^\circ-A)=-\cos A$.
answer.worked:
Let $X$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $AC$ extended, with $BX=h$ and $XA=x$.

In right-angled $\triangle BXA$:
$$\begin{align*}c^2&=h^2+x^2\\h^2&=c^2-x^2\end{align*}$$
Since $\angle BAX=180^\circ-A$,
$$\begin{align*}x&=c\cos(180^\circ-A)\\x&=-c\cos A\end{align*}$$
In right-angled $\triangle BXC$, $XC=b+x$. Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}a^2&=(b+x)^2+h^2\\a^2&=b^2+2bx+x^2+c^2-x^2\\a^2&=b^2+c^2+2bx\\a^2&=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A\end{align*}$$
Thus the cosine rule also holds when $A$ is obtuse.

content.prompt: A triangle has sides of length 9 cm, 13 cm and 18 cm. Calculate the size of the largest angle, correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
The largest angle $\theta$ is opposite the longest side, 18 cm.

$$\begin{align*}18^2&=9^2+13^2-2\times9\times13\cos\theta\\\cos\theta&=\frac{9^2+13^2-18^2}{2\times9\times13}\\\cos\theta&=-\frac{37}{117}\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{37}{117}\right)\\\theta&\approx108.4^\circ\end{align*}$$

The largest angle is $108.4^\circ$, correct to one decimal place.

content.prompt: Find all the angles of a triangle whose sides are in the ratio $4:8:11$, to the nearest degree.

answer.short:
$16^\circ$, $34^\circ$, $130^\circ$, opposite the sides in the ratio $4$, $8$, $11$, respectively.

Use proportional side lengths in the cosine rule.
answer.worked:
Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be opposite sides $4k$, $8k$ and $11k$, respectively, where $k>0$.

$$\begin{align*}\cos A&=\frac{(8k)^2+(11k)^2-(4k)^2}{2(8k)(11k)}\\\cos A&=\frac{169}{176}\\A&\approx16.2136335^\circ\\\cos B&=\frac{(4k)^2+(11k)^2-(8k)^2}{2(4k)(11k)}\\\cos B&=\frac{73}{88}\\B&\approx33.9479265^\circ\\C&=180^\circ-A-B\\C&\approx129.8384400^\circ\end{align*}$$

Use the unrounded values of $A$ and $B$ when calculating $C$. To the nearest degree, the angles are $16^\circ$, $34^\circ$ and $130^\circ$.

answer.worked:
The longer diagonal forms a triangle with sides 12 cm, 18 cm and 22 cm. Its angle $\theta$ opposite the diagonal is the obtuse angle of the parallelogram.

$$\begin{align*}22^2&=12^2+18^2-2\times12\times18\cos\theta\\\cos\theta&=\frac{12^2+18^2-22^2}{2\times12\times18}\\\cos\theta&=-\frac{1}{27}\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{27}\right)\\\theta&\approx92.1^\circ\end{align*}$$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\cos\angle ACB&=\frac{10^2+14^2-6^2}{2\times10\times14}\\\cos\angle ACB&=\frac{13}{14}\\\angle ACB&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{13}{14}\right)\\\angle ACB&\approx21.8^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii

answer.worked:
$CX=7\text{ cm}$ because $X$ is the midpoint of $BC$. Since $\angle ACX=\angle ACB$, use the exact value $\cos\angle ACX=\frac{13}{14}$.

$$\begin{align*}AX^2&=10^2+7^2-2\times10\times7\times\frac{13}{14}\\AX^2&=19\\AX&=\sqrt{19}\text{ cm}\\AX&\approx4.4\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: of the triangle. A median is the line segment from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
Find the length of the other two medians, correct to one decimal place.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with horizontal CB, A above the base, median AX, matching single ticks on CX and XB, and a red midpoint X. No numerical measurements are printed.
spec.mathematics: X is the midpoint of BC; CX=XB and AX joins A to X. Coordinates are derived from the given side lengths.
spec.answerVisibility: All labels, midpoint ticks and the median are permanent question givens; no calculated answers appear.

answer.short:
The median from $B$ is $9.5\text{ cm}$; the median from $C$ is $11.8\text{ cm}$.

Bisect the relevant side and apply the cosine rule.
answer.worked:
Let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$ and $E$ the midpoint of $AB$. Then $AD=5\text{ cm}$ and $BE=3\text{ cm}$.

For the median from $B$:

$$\begin{align*}\cos A&=\frac{6^2+10^2-14^2}{2\times6\times10}\\\cos A&=-\frac12\\BD^2&=6^2+5^2-2\times6\times5\times\left(-\frac12\right)\\BD^2&=91\\BD&=\sqrt{91}\text{ cm}\\BD&\approx9.5\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

For the median from $C$:

$$\begin{align*}\cos B&=\frac{6^2+14^2-10^2}{2\times6\times14}\\\cos B&=\frac{11}{14}\\CE^2&=14^2+3^2-2\times14\times3\times\frac{11}{14}\\CE^2&=139\\CE&=\sqrt{139}\text{ cm}\\CE&\approx11.8\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use the sine rule to find $\angle CAB$, correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{20}{\sin\angle CAB}&=\frac{16}{\sin50^\circ}\\\frac{\sin\angle CAB}{20}&=\frac{\sin50^\circ}{16}\\\sin\angle CAB&=\frac{20\sin50^\circ}{16}\\\angle CAB&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{20\sin50^\circ}{16}\right)\\\angle CAB&\approx73.2^\circ\end{align*}$$
The acute solution is required.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find $\angle ABC$, correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
Angles in a triangle sum to $180^\circ$. Using the unrounded result from part a:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABC&=180^\circ-50^\circ-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{20\sin50^\circ}{16}\right)\\\angle ABC&\approx56.8^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the area of the triangle, correct to the nearest square centimetre.

answer.worked:
Use the unrounded value of $\angle ABC$, the included angle between the known sides.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area}&=\frac12\times16\times20\times\sin\angle ABC\\\text{Area}&=160\sin\left(130^\circ-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{20\sin50^\circ}{16}\right)\right)\\\text{Area}&\approx134\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
The third angle is $\theta$:

spec.description: Unshaded quadrilateral ABCD with A lower left, B above and slightly right of A, C upper right and D directly below C. No diagonal is supplied. Ordinary blue source strokes become house black.

children.label: a
children.prompt: the length $AC$

answer.worked:
In right-angled triangle $ADC$, by Pythagoras’ theorem:
$$\begin{align*}AC^2&=80^2+130^2\\AC^2&=23300\\AC&=\sqrt{23300}\\AC&\approx152.6\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: $\angle ABC$

answer.worked:
Apply the cosine rule in triangle $ABC$, retaining $AC^2=23300$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\angle ABC&=\frac{65^2+90^2-23300}{2(65)(90)}\\\cos\angle ABC&=-\frac{439}{468}\\\angle ABC&=\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{439}{468}\right)\\\angle ABC&\approx159.7^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: the area of the block

answer.short:
$6213.6\text{ m}^2$.

Split along $AC$ and add the areas of triangles $ADC$ and $ABC$.
answer.worked:
Split the block along $AC$. Let $\theta=\cos^{-1}(-439/468)$, the unrounded angle from part b.
$$\begin{align*}A_{ADC}&=\frac12(80)(130)\\A_{ADC}&=5200\text{ m}^2\\A_{ABC}&=\frac12(65)(90)\sin\theta\\A_{ABCD}&=5200+\frac12(65)(90)\sin\left(\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{439}{468}\right)\right)\\A_{ABCD}&\approx6213.6\text{ m}^2.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A quadrilateral has diagonals of length $12\text{ cm}$ and $18\text{ cm}$. If the angle between the diagonals is $65^\circ$, find the area of the quadrilateral, correct to the nearest square centimetre.

answer.short:
$98\text{ cm}^2$.

Split the quadrilateral into four triangles at the diagonal intersection and apply the triangle area rule.
answer.worked:
Let the diagonals intersect at $O$. Let the two segments of one diagonal have lengths $x$ and $y$, and those of the other have lengths $u$ and $v$, in centimetres. Thus $x+y=12$ and $u+v=18$.

The four angles at $O$ alternate between $65^\circ$ and $115^\circ$. Since $\sin115^\circ=\sin65^\circ$, adding the four triangle areas gives:
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12xu\sin65^\circ+\frac12yu\sin65^\circ+\frac12yv\sin65^\circ+\frac12xv\sin65^\circ\\A&=\frac12(x+y)(u+v)\sin65^\circ\\A&=\frac12(12)(18)\sin65^\circ\\A&=108\sin65^\circ\text{ cm}^2\\A&\approx98\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: The sides of a triangle $ABC$ are enlarged by a factor, $k$. Use the area formula to show that the area is enlarged by the factor, $k^2$.

answer.short:
$A'=\frac12(ka)(kb)\sin C=k^2A$.

The included angle is unchanged, so the area is enlarged by the factor $k^2$.
answer.worked:
Let the original area be $A=\frac12ab\sin C$. Enlargement preserves the included angle $C$, while the two sides become $ka$ and $kb$.

$$\begin{align*}A'&=\frac12(ka)(kb)\sin C\\A'&=k^2\left(\frac12ab\sin C\right)\\A'&=k^2A.\end{align*}$$

Therefore the area is enlarged by the factor $k^2$.

content.prompt: Prove that the formula $\text{Area}=\frac12ab\sin C$ gives the area of a triangle when $C$ is obtuse.

answer.short:
$\text{Area}=\frac12ah=\frac12ab\sin(180^\circ-C)=\frac12ab\sin C$.

Drop a perpendicular to the extension of the base and use the equality of the sines of supplementary angles.
answer.worked:
In $\triangle ABC$, let $BC=a$, $CA=b$ and $\angle ACB=C$ be obtuse. Extend $BC$ beyond $C$ to $P$ and draw $AP\perp BP$, with $AP=h$.

Since $CP$ and $CB$ point in opposite directions, $\angle ACP=180^\circ-C$. In right-angled triangle $ACP$:
$$\begin{align*}\sin(180^\circ-C)&=\frac{h}{b}\\h&=b\sin(180^\circ-C)\\h&=b\sin C.\end{align*}$$
The last equality uses the fact that supplementary angles have equal sines. Using base $BC=a$ and perpendicular height $h$:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area of }\triangle ABC&=\frac12ah\\\text{Area of }\triangle ABC&=\frac12a\bigl(b\sin C\bigr)\\\text{Area of }\triangle ABC&=\frac12ab\sin C.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Write down two formulas for the area of triangle $ABC$ and deduce the sine rule from those two formulas.

spec.sourceRegion: Challenge exercise question 1, triangle to the right of the instruction
spec.description: Unshaded triangle with A above, B lower left and C lower right; side labels lie outside their corresponding edges. Ordinary source blue strokes are rendered in house black.
spec.mathematics: BC=a, AC=b, AB=c; each lowercase side is opposite its corresponding uppercase vertex.
spec.answerVisibility: All vertex and side labels are permanent givens; no answer annotations are supplied.

answer.short:
$K=\frac12 ab\sin C$ and $K=\frac12 ac\sin B$, so $\displaystyle\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}$.

Equate the two area formulas and divide by the common factors.
answer.worked:
Let the area of triangle $ABC$ be $K$.

$$\begin{align*}K&=\frac12 ab\sin C\\K&=\frac12 ac\sin B\end{align*}$$

Equating these expressions gives

$$\begin{align*}\frac12 ab\sin C&=\frac12 ac\sin B\\b\sin C&=c\sin B\\\frac{b}{\sin B}&=\frac{c}{\sin C}.\end{align*}$$

This is the sine rule for the opposite pairs $(b,B)$ and $(c,C)$.

content.prompt: Simi is standing 200 metres due east of Ricardo. From Ricardo, the angle of elevation from the ground to the top of a building due north of Ricardo is $12^\circ$. From Simi, the angle of elevation from the ground to the top of the building is $9^\circ$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Let the height of the building be $h$ metres. Express the following in terms of $h$:

children.label: i
children.prompt: the distance from Ricardo to the foot of the building

answer.worked:
Let $R$ be Ricardo's position and $F$ the foot of the building.
$$\begin{align*}\tan12^\circ&=\frac{h}{RF}\\RF\tan12^\circ&=h\\RF&=\frac{h}{\tan12^\circ}\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: the distance from Simi to the foot of the building

answer.worked:
Let $S$ be Simi's position and $F$ the foot of the building.
$$\begin{align*}\tan9^\circ&=\frac{h}{SF}\\SF\tan9^\circ&=h\\SF&=\frac{h}{\tan9^\circ}\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use your answers to part a and Pythagoras’ theorem to find the height of the building correct to one decimal place.

answer.short:
$47.5\text{ m}$

Apply Pythagoras’ theorem to the horizontal triangle using the distances from part a.
answer.worked:
Let $R$, $S$ and $F$ denote Ricardo, Simi and the foot of the building. Since $RF$ is north and $RS$ is east, $\angle FRS=90^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}SF^2&=RF^2+RS^2\\\left(\frac{h}{\tan9^\circ}\right)^2&=\left(\frac{h}{\tan12^\circ}\right)^2+200^2\\h^2\left(\frac{1}{\tan^2 9^\circ}-\frac{1}{\tan^2 12^\circ}\right)&=40000\\h^2&=\frac{40000}{\frac{1}{\tan^2 9^\circ}-\frac{1}{\tan^2 12^\circ}}\\h&=\frac{200}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{\tan^2 9^\circ}-\frac{1}{\tan^2 12^\circ}}}\\h&\approx47.5\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: On what bearing is the building from Simi? Give your answer to the nearest degree.

answer.short:
$318^\circ\mathrm{T}$

Find the angle west of north, then subtract it from $360^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Using the unrounded height from part b, the northward distance is $RF=h/\tan12^\circ$. Let $\theta$ be the angle west of north from Simi to the building.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{200}{h/\tan12^\circ}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{200\tan12^\circ}{h}\right)\\\theta&\approx41.828857^\circ\\\text{Bearing}&=360^\circ-\theta\\\text{Bearing}&\approx318^\circ\mathrm{T}.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:

Substitute $c=a\sin C/\sin A$ from the sine rule.
answer.worked:

Using the area rule,
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area}&=\frac12 ac\sin B\\\text{Area}&=\frac12 a\left(\frac{a\sin C}{\sin A}\right)\sin B\\\text{Area}&=\frac{a^2\sin B\sin C}{2\sin A}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Here is an alternative proof of the cosine rule. Assume $\triangle ABC$ is acute-angled.

spec.description: Acute triangle with red dashed altitude and right-angle marker; the foot remains unlabelled in the question.
spec.mathematics: BC=a, AC=b, AB=c. Altitude from A meets the interior of BC perpendicularly.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry and side labels are visible.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that $a=b\cos C+c\cos B$.

answer.short: $a=BD+DC=c\cos B+b\cos C$, where $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $A$.
answer.worked:
Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$. Right-triangle cosine ratios give $BD=c\cos B$ and $DC=b\cos C$.
$$\begin{align*}a&=BD+DC\\a&=c\cos B+b\cos C\\a&=b\cos C+c\cos B.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Write down corresponding results for $b$ and $c$.

answer.worked:
Applying the same projection argument to the other two sides gives
$$\begin{align*}b&=a\cos C+c\cos A,\\c&=a\cos B+b\cos A.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that $a^2=a(b\cos C+c\cos B)$ and, using corresponding results for $b^2$ and $c^2$, prove the cosine rule.

answer.short:
$a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$.

Multiply the three projection identities by their respective side lengths, then combine $b^2+c^2-a^2$.
answer.worked:
Multiply each projection identity by its left-hand side:
$$\begin{align*}a^2&=a(b\cos C+c\cos B)\\a^2&=ab\cos C+ac\cos B,\\b^2&=ab\cos C+bc\cos A,\\c^2&=ac\cos B+bc\cos A.\end{align*}$$
Subtract the expression for $a^2$ from the sum of the other two:
$$\begin{align*}b^2+c^2-a^2&=(ab\cos C+bc\cos A)+(ac\cos B+bc\cos A)-(ab\cos C+ac\cos B)\\b^2+c^2-a^2&=2bc\cos A,\\a^2&=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Check that a similar proof works for an obtuse-angled triangle.

answer.short: The projection identities still hold because $\cos(180^\circ-B)=-\cos B$ when $B$ is obtuse. The same cancellation proves $a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$.
answer.worked:
Suppose $B$ is obtuse. Let the perpendicular from $A$ meet the extension of $BC$ beyond $B$ at $D$. Then
$$\begin{align*}BD&=c\cos(180^\circ-B)\\BD&=-c\cos B,\\CD&=b\cos C,\\a&=CD-BD\\a&=b\cos C+c\cos B.\end{align*}$$
The angle $A$ is acute, so the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$ meets $AB$ extended beyond $B$. The same subtraction of projections gives $c=b\cos A+a\cos B$. The perpendicular from $B$ to $AC$ gives $b=a\cos C+c\cos A$. Thus all three identities remain valid. Multiplying by $a$, $b$ and $c$ respectively and combining them as in part c gives
$$\begin{align*}b^2+c^2-a^2&=2bc\cos A,\\a^2&=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A.\end{align*}$$
Relabelling covers an obtuse angle at either of the other vertices.

content.prompt: $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle, with $AB=AC=1$. Suppose $\angle BAC=2\theta$.

spec.description: Unfilled isosceles triangle with equal-side ticks, the whole apex angle marked 2 theta, and a red dashed apex-to-base-midpoint segment. No right-angle marker is added.
spec.mathematics: AB=AC=1 from the stem; the dashed segment bisects the apex angle and the base.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $BC^2=2(1-\cos2\theta)$.

answer.worked:
By the cosine rule,
$$\begin{align*}BC^2&=1^2+1^2-2(1)(1)\cos2\theta\\BC^2&=2-2\cos2\theta\\BC^2&=2(1-\cos2\theta).\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that $BC=2\sin\theta$.

answer.worked:
Let $D$ be the midpoint of $BC$. In an isosceles triangle, $AD$ is perpendicular to $BC$ and bisects $\angle BAC$, so $\angle BAD=\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{BD}{1},\\BD&=\sin\theta,\\BC&=2BD\\BC&=2\sin\theta.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Deduce that $1-\cos2\theta=2(\sin\theta)^2$.

answer.worked:
Equating the expressions for $BC^2$ from parts a and b gives
$$\begin{align*}2(1-\cos2\theta)&=(2\sin\theta)^2\\2(1-\cos2\theta)&=4\sin^2\theta,\\1-\cos2\theta&=2\sin^2\theta.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Deduce that $\cos2\theta=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta$.

answer.worked:
Use $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos2\theta&=1-2\sin^2\theta\\\cos2\theta&=(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)-2\sin^2\theta\\\cos2\theta&=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta.\end{align*}$$

$$1+\cos A=\frac{(b+c)^2-a^2}{2bc},\qquad 1-\cos A=\frac{a^2-(b-c)^2}{2bc}.$$

Rearrange the cosine rule, then combine each expression over the denominator $2bc$.
answer.worked:
The cosine rule gives
$$\begin{align*}a^2&=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A,\\\cos A&=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}.\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}1+\cos A&=\frac{2bc+b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc},\\1+\cos A&=\frac{(b+c)^2-a^2}{2bc},\\1-\cos A&=\frac{2bc-b^2-c^2+a^2}{2bc},\\1-\cos A&=\frac{a^2-(b-c)^2}{2bc}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Let $s=\dfrac{a+b+c}{2}$.

Show that
$$1+\cos A=\frac{2s(s-a)}{bc}$$
and
$$1-\cos A=\frac{2(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}.$$

answer.short:
$$1+\cos A=\frac{2s(s-a)}{bc},\qquad 1-\cos A=\frac{2(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}.$$

Factor the numerators in part a and use $2s=a+b+c$.
answer.worked:
Since $2s=a+b+c$,
$$\begin{align*}b+c-a&=2(s-a),\\a-b+c&=2(s-b),\\a+b-c&=2(s-c).\end{align*}$$
Using part a,
$$\begin{align*}1+\cos A&=\frac{(b+c-a)(b+c+a)}{2bc},\\1+\cos A&=\frac{2(s-a)\cdot2s}{2bc},\\1+\cos A&=\frac{2s(s-a)}{bc},\\1-\cos A&=\frac{(a-b+c)(a+b-c)}{2bc},\\1-\cos A&=\frac{2(s-b)\cdot2(s-c)}{2bc},\\1-\cos A&=\frac{2(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt:
Use the fact that $(\sin A)^2=1-(\cos A)^2$ to show that the square of the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$ and deduce Heron’s formula for the area of a triangle:
$$\text{Area}=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}.$$

answer.short:
$$\text{Area}^2=s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c),\qquad \text{Area}=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}.$$

Multiply the identities in part b and use $\text{Area}=\tfrac12bc\sin A$.
answer.worked:
Using part b,
$$\begin{align*}\sin^2 A&=(1+\cos A)(1-\cos A),\\\sin^2 A&=\frac{2s(s-a)}{bc}\cdot\frac{2(s-b)(s-c)}{bc},\\\sin^2 A&=\frac{4s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}{b^2c^2}.\end{align*}$$
Let the area be $K$. By the triangle area rule,
$$\begin{align*}K&=\frac12bc\sin A,\\K^2&=\frac14b^2c^2\sin^2 A,\\K^2&=s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c),\\K&=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}.\end{align*}$$
Take the positive square root because the area is positive.

content.prompt: Given two sides and a non-included angle, describe the conditions for 0, 1, or 2 triangles to exist.

answer.short:
Let $A$ be the given angle, $a$ its opposite side, $b$ the other given side, and $h=b\sin A$.

For acute $A$: 0 triangles if $a<h$; 1 if $a=h$ or $a\ge b$; 2 if $h<a<b$.

For $A\ge90^\circ$: 0 triangles if $a\le b$; 1 if $a>b$. There are never 2.

Compare the opposite side with the altitude and the other given side.
answer.worked:
Let $A$ be the given angle, $a$ the opposite side and $b$ the other given side. The perpendicular height is $h=b\sin A$.

If $A$ is acute:

• $a<h$: the side of length $a$ cannot reach the opposite ray, so there are 0 triangles.

• $a=h$: it meets the ray at the perpendicular foot, giving 1 right-angled triangle.

• $h<a<b$: it reaches the ray in two positions, giving 2 triangles.

• $a\ge b$: only one non-degenerate position is possible, giving 1 triangle.

If $A$ is right or obtuse, its opposite side must be longer than $b$. Thus $a>b$ gives 1 triangle, while $a\le b$ gives 0 triangles.

The sine rule confirms the possible second angle:
$$\sin B=\frac{b\sin A}{a}.$$
An acute candidate $B$ and its supplement are both valid only when each leaves $A+B<180^\circ$.

entries.description:
Trigonometry begins with the study of relationships between sides and angles in a right-angled triangle.

In this chapter, we will review the basics of the trigonometry of right-angled triangles, look at applications to three-dimensional problems, and extend our study of trigonometry to triangles that are not right-angled.

entries.description:
By similarity, the ratio of any two sides in a right-angled triangle is always the same, once we have fixed the angles.
We choose one of the two acute angles and call it the reference angle.
The side opposite the reference angle is called the opposite, the side opposite the right angle is called the hypotenuse and the remaining side, which is between the reference angle and the right-angle, is called the adjacent.

entries.description:
The three basic trigonometric ratios are the sine, cosine and tangent ratios.
\(\sin\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), \(\cos\theta=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), \(\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\).
You should learn the three ratios for sine, cosine and tangent by heart and remember them. A simple mnemonic is:
SOHCAHTOA
for Sine: Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cosine: Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tangent: Opposite/Adjacent

entries.description:
In the diagram, the angles at A and B are complementary; that is, they add to 90°.
The side opposite A is the side adjacent to B and vice versa. Hence, the sine of θ is the cosine of (90° − θ) and vice versa.
\(\sin\theta=\cos(90^\circ-\theta)\)
\(\cos\theta=\sin(90^\circ-\theta)\)
For example, sin 60° = cos 30° and cos 10° = sin 80°.

entries.description:
In order to apply trigonometry to finding angles rather than side lengths in right-angled triangles, we need to be able to go from the value of sine, cosine or tangent back to the angle.

What is the acute angle whose sine is 0.5?

The calculator gives sin 30° = 0.5, so we write sin⁻¹ 0.5 = 30°.

The opposite process of finding the sine of an angle is to find the inverse sine of a number.

When θ is an acute angle, the statement sin⁻¹ x = θ means sin θ = x.

This notation is standard, but is rather misleading. The index −1 does NOT mean one over, as it normally does in algebra. To help you avoid confusion, you should always read sin⁻¹ x as inverse sine of x and tan⁻¹ x as inverse tan of x, and so on.

For example, the calculator gives cos⁻¹ 0.8192 ≈ 35° (read this as inverse cosine of 0.8192 is approximately 35°).

When a person looks at an object that is higher than the person’s eye, the angle between the line of sight and the horizontal is called the angle of elevation.
On the other hand, when the object is lower than the person’s eye, the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight is called the angle of depression.

entries.description:
Bearings are used to indicate the direction of an object from a fixed reference point, O.
True bearings give the angle θ° from north, measured clockwise. We write a true bearing of θ° as θ°T, where θ° is an angle between 0° and 360°. It is customary to write the angle using three digits, so 0°T is written 000°T, 15°T is written 015°T, and so on.
For example, in the diagram opposite, the true bearing of A from O is 060°T, and the true bearing of B from O is 140°T.

entries.description:
In many situations we encounter triangles that are not right-angled. We can use trigonometry to deal with these triangles as well. One of the two key formulas for doing this is known as the sine rule.
We begin with an acute-angled triangle, ABC, with side lengths a, b and c, as shown below. (It is standard to write a lower case letter on a side and the corresponding upper case letter on the angle opposite that side.) Drop a perpendicular, CP, of length h, from C to AB.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation introducing the sine-rule derivation; no practice task.

entries.description: Acute triangle ABC: B at lower left, A at lower right and C above the base. BC is labelled a, CA is labelled b. Perpendicular CP meets BA at P, with h beside CP and a right-angle marker at P. A double-headed dimension arrow below BA is labelled c.
entries.presentation: Blue triangle edges and altitude; black labels, right-angle marker and dimension arrow. Diagram appears between the introductory text and derivation.
entries.exclusionReason: Mathematically meaningful diagram supporting standalone teaching; retain as taught-method evidence.

entries.description:
In ΔAPC we have sin A = h/b, so h = b sin A.
Similarly, in ΔCPB we have sin B = h/a, so h = a sin B.
Equating these expressions for h, we have:
b sin A = a sin B
which we can write as:
a/sin A = b/sin B
The same result holds for the side c and angle C, so we can write:
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
This is known as the sine rule.
In words, this says ‘any side of a triangle over the sine of the opposite angle equals any other side of the triangle over the sine of its opposite angle’.
This result also holds in an obtuse-angled triangle. We will look at that case later.
entries.presentation: Fractions use stacked native mathematics. The three displayed equalities are blue-violet; the words “sine rule” are bold pink-red.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone derivation and definition; reference evidence only.

entries.description:
In any triangle ABC:
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
For example, the sine rule can be used to find an unknown length of a side of a triangle when a side length and the angles are known. This is closely related to the AAS congruence test.

entries.description: Trigonometric ratios of obtuse angles
entries.presentation: Main topic band.

entries.description:
We have seen that we can use the sine rule to find sides and angles in acute-angled triangles. What happens when one of the angles is obtuse? We can extend our definition of the basic trigonometric functions to obtuse angles by using coordinate geometry.

We begin by drawing a circle of radius 1 in the Cartesian plane, with its centre at the origin. The equation of the circle is x² + y² = 1.

Take a point P(a, b) on the circle in the first quadrant and form the right-angled triangle POQ with O at the origin. Let ∠POQ be θ.

cos θ = OQ/OP = a/1 = a, and
sin θ = QP/OP = b/1 = b

But a is the x-coordinate of P and b is the y-coordinate of P.

Hence, the coordinates of the point P are (cos θ, sin θ).
entries.presentation: Editable native mathematics, with stacked fractions in the two displayed equations. First unit-circle diagram sits to the right.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone derivation of the unit-circle definitions; no practice question.

entries.description:
Now take θ to be 30°, so P has coordinates (cos 30°, sin 30°).

Suppose that we move the point P around the circle to P′ so that P′ makes an angle of 150° with the positive x-axis. (Recall that 30° and 150° are supplementary angles.)

The coordinates of P′ are (cos 150°, sin 150°). But we can see that triangles OPQ and OP′Q′ are congruent, so the y-coordinates of P and P′ are the same. That is:

sin 150° = sin 30°

The x-coordinates have the same magnitude but opposite sign, so:

cos 150° = −cos 30°

From this example, we can see the following rules.

entries.description:
We know, from the SAS congruence test, that a triangle is completely determined if we are given two of its sides and the included angle. If we want to know the third side and the two other angles, the sine rule does not help us.
You can see from the diagram that there is not enough information to apply the sine rule. This is because the known angle is not opposite one of the known sides.
Fortunately there is another rule called the cosine rule which we can use in this situation.

entries.description:
Suppose that ABC is a triangle and that the angles A and C are acute. Drop a perpendicular from B to AC and mark the side lengths as shown in the diagram.
In ΔBDA, Pythagoras’ theorem tells us that:
c² = h² + (b − x)²
Also in ΔCBD, by Pythagoras’ theorem we have:
h² = a² − x²
Substituting this expression for h² into the first equation and expanding:
c² = a² − x²(b − x)²
   = a² − x² + b² − 2bx + x²
   = a² + b² − 2bx
Finally, from ΔCBD, we have x/a = cos C. That is, x = a cos C and so:
c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone derivation of the cosine rule; reference evidence only.

presentation.text: 12G Finding angles using the cosine rule

entries.description:
The SSS congruence test tells us that once three sides of a triangle are known, the angles are uniquely determined. The question is, how do we find them?
Given three sides of a triangle, we can substitute the information into the cosine rule and rearrange to find the cosine of one of the angles and hence the angle.
If you prefer, you can learn or derive another form of the cosine rule, with cos C as the subject.
Rearranging c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C we have:
2ab cos C = a² + b² − c²
cos C = (a² + b² − c²)/(2ab)
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation and formula derivation; retain as taught-method evidence only.

entries.description:
The smallest angle in the triangle is opposite the smallest side.
Applying the cosine rule:
6² = 8² + 11² − 2 × 8 × 11 × cos θ
cos θ = (8² + 11² − 6²)/(2 × 8 × 11)
= 149/172
and so θ ≈ 32.2° (Correct to one decimal place.)
